questions.question: Quantitative microscopy CANNOT quantify the following :

explanations.a: Incorrect — voids can be quantified using area fraction, size distribution, and porosity measurements in quantitative microscopy.
explanations.b: Correct — matrix is the continuous background phase; quantitative microscopy focuses on discrete features (like pores, particles, phases), so the matrix itself is not directly quantified as a feature.
explanations.c: Incorrect — reinforcement phases can be quantified in composites (volume fraction, size, distribution).
explanations.d: Incorrect — compositional differences can be analyzed using image analysis and linked techniques, so they are not excluded from quantitative evaluation.

questions.question: Interpretation of 3-D quantitative information from a 2-D structure or length or point analysis is called :

explanations.a: Correct — Stereology is the method used to interpret 3D quantitative microstructural information from 2D sections using statistical and geometrical analysis.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Tessellation refers to tiling patterns in geometry, not microstructural analysis.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Biology is a broad scientific field and not a specific method for 3D interpretation from 2D data.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Telegraphy is a communication method and has no relation to materials characterization.

questions.question: The difference between the light intensity of the specimen and its background is called :

explanations.a: Incorrect — brightness refers to the overall light intensity of an image, not the difference between regions.
explanations.b: Correct — contrast is the difference in light intensity between the specimen and its background, which helps in distinguishing microstructural features.
explanations.c: Incorrect — saturation refers to color intensity in colored images, not intensity difference in grayscale optical microscopy.
explanations.d: Incorrect — diffraction is a wave phenomenon related to light interaction with structures, not image intensity difference.

questions.question: Using a 40 × objective, 20 divisions on the eyepiece graticule correspond to 10 divisions on the stage micrometer. If one division of stage micrometer is 100 µm, what is the length of a single eyepiece graticule division at this magnification ?

explanations.a: Incorrect — this value is too small; calibration shows each eyepiece division is larger than 10 µm.
explanations.b: Incorrect — 20 µm does not match the given stage micrometer calibration relationship.
explanations.c: Correct — 10 stage divisions = 1000 µm, which corresponds to 20 eyepiece divisions, so 1 eyepiece division = 50 µm.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 200 µm is too large and inconsistent with the calibration ratio provided.

questions.question: What is the significance of using scale bar on a micrograph (in quantitative optical microscopy) ?

answers.a: It provides the total magnification used to capture the micrograph
answers.b: It is only required for electron microscopy images
answers.c: It shows the actual size of the objects and remains accurate even if the image is resized
answers.d: It indicates the refractive index of the medium surrounding the specimen

explanations.a: Incorrect — magnification can change if the image is resized, while the scale bar represents actual length, not magnification.
explanations.b: Incorrect — scale bars are required in both optical and electron microscopy, not only electron microscopy.
explanations.c: Correct — a scale bar represents the real physical size of features in the image and remains valid even if the image is resized proportionally.
explanations.d: Incorrect — refractive index is unrelated to scale bars and is not indicated in micrographs this way.
